title: Ro Khanna Holds More Campaign Cash Than Seven Lawmakers Combined
excerpt: FEC records as reported show the California Democrat with about $16.6 million and no debt, against roughly $11.1 million combined for the other seven Indian-American House members and members-elect.
body:
• Representative Ro Khanna reported about $16.6 million in campaign cash with no outstanding debt, the largest balance among eight Indian-American House members and members-elect, according to a review of Federal Election Commission records.
  • That single balance exceeds the roughly $11.1 million held by the other seven combined — a gap of about $5.5 million.
  • Shri Thanedar held the second-largest cash balance, about $5.9 million as of September 30, but reported $14.44 million in campaign debt, more than twice his cash.
  • Figures are snapshots from different reporting dates in the 2026 cycle — Khanna's through October 14, others as of September 30 — so treat them as a comparison of filings, not a single-day league table.

US Representative Ro Khanna has more campaign cash than the other seven Indian-American lawmakers and members-elect in the comparison combined, according to a review of Federal Election Commission (FEC) records reported by India Weekly and in an IANS report carried by BizzBuzz.

Khanna, a California Democrat, reported approximately $16.6 million in campaign cash and no outstanding debt. The other seven collectively held around $11.1 million.

Khanna's cycle in numbers

During the 2026 election cycle through October 14, Khanna's campaign received $15.3 million and spent $9.5 million, both reports said. His accumulated cash balance is higher than his receipts in that period, which simply means the $16.6 million includes money carried into the cycle, not only money raised during it — an important distinction before comparing balances with receipts.

Cash on hand is not the same as money raised, and neither report treats it as such. It is the balance a campaign has available at the reporting date, after spending.

The rest of the incumbents

Representative Shri Thanedar held the second-largest reserve, approximately $5.9 million as of September 30. The other side of his ledger is larger: his campaign reported $14.44 million in debt, received $3.2 million and spent $4.2 million during the cycle.

Representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington reported approximately $1.75 million in cash, with receipts of $2.9 million and spending of $3.2 million and no debt. California Representative Ami Bera held around $1.65 million, reported $80,000 in debt, and took in $1.5 million against $1.7 million in spending. Virginia Representative Suhas Subramanyam reported approximately $746,000 in cash and no debt, having raised $1.7 million and spent about $1.1 million.

Two accounts, and a warning about adding them up

Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi's finances were split across two campaigns. As of September 30, his House account held about $47,000 and his Senate account about $33,000. The House account reported $3.9 million in receipts and $21 million in expenditures; the Senate campaign reported $31.6 million in receipts and $31.5 million in spending.

Both reports flag the same accounting caution, and it is the key to reading that Senate figure: $19.4 million of the Senate receipts consisted of transfers from other authorised committees. Money moved between a politician's own authorised accounts can be counted more than once if receipts are simply added together, so the $31.6 million is not $31.6 million of new fundraising.

The members-elect

The two newly elected members reported smaller balances from before their victories. Amish Shah, who defeated Republican Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st Congressional District, reported receipts of $5.7 million and disbursements of $5.5 million through October 14, leaving about $206,000 in cash and nearly $37,000 in debt.

Pia Dandiya, who defeated Republican Casey Askar in Florida's 22nd District, reported $4.6 million in receipts and $3.9 million in spending, with about $735,000 remaining and $247,000 in debt.

Taken together, the FEC filings as reported show a wide spread inside a small group: one debt-free $16.6 million balance at the top, a second-largest balance outweighed by its own campaign's debt, and first-time winners who spent most of what they raised to get elected. All of the figures above are approximate, as reported from the filings, and they date from September 30 or October 14 rather than a single common day.
